title: Many-body entanglement quantification in arbitrary states through a few partial-transpose moments
abstract: Can the entanglement of an arbitrary many-body state be quantified without reconstructing the state? We answer the question affirmatively by showing how the measure of logarithmic negativity can be estimated using a finite number of even partial transpose (PT) moments of a many-body state. Considering the squared PT spectrum as a probability measure, we solve exactly the task of a truncated Hausdorff moment problem with Gauss and Gauss-Radau quadrature. We obtain a hierarchy of lower bounds on the logarithmic negativity, which improves with increasing order of moments. Convergence to the exact value of the measure can be achieved for every state of finite dimension. We illustrate the bounds for ground states of three different interacting spin models, as well as for a thermal state. An error analysis demonstrates the efficacy of our scheme towards handling the limitation of finite statistics encountered in actual experiments with randomized measurements. Moreover, an example of density matrix renormalization group based numerical estimation is provided for handling system sizes beyond the scope of exact diagonalization.
summary: This work develops a theoretical framework to estimate entanglement, specifically the logarithmic negativity, using only a finite set of measurable partial-transpose moments. By framing the problem as solving a truncated moment problem, the authors establish a rigorous hierarchy of lower bounds that converge to the exact entanglement value for any finite system. This offers a practical pathway for characterizing entanglement in complex quantum materials and systems.
main_problem: The central problem is quantifying the entanglement of an arbitrary many-body quantum state without needing to reconstruct the full state density matrix.
main_result: The logarithmic negativity can be accurately estimated by solving a truncated Hausdorff moment problem using a finite number of measurable even partial-transpose moments.
method: The method involves establishing a hierarchy of lower bounds ($E_4 \le E_6 \le E_8 \le \dots$) on the logarithmic negativity by treating the squared partial-transpose spectrum as a probability measure and applying Gauss/Gauss-Radau quadrature.
model_or_system: The theory is applied to general many-body quantum states, including ground states of interacting spin models (TFIM, XXZ, LMG) and thermal states.
key_observables: Logarithmic negativity ($E(ho)$), partial-transpose moments ($p_k(ho)$), and the derived lower bounds ($E_{2K}(ho)$).
important_parameters: The order of the moment ($K$), the system size ($n$), and the coupling/field parameters ($h, \Delta, T$) of the tested Hamiltonians.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the entanglement measure can be bounded by moments derived from the partial transpose, and that the state is finite-dimensional, guaranteeing convergence.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the convergence of the moment bounds ($E_4, E_6, E_8$) towards the true entanglement measure ($E$) for various spin models (TFIM, XXZ, LMG) and thermal states.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, develops the moment-based bounding technique using moment theory, proves the convergence and monotonicity of the bounds, and then validates the method by applying it to several canonical quantum spin models.
why_interesting: This provides a powerful, experimentally relevant tool to estimate complex entanglement measures using only measurable quantities (moments), bypassing the need for full state tomography, which is crucial for large quantum systems.

Figure 2 shows the result. The ordering of Eq. (14) holds at every scanned point of the three models. In the TFIM all quantifiers vanish for h →0, where the ground state is a cat state and the reduced state of AB is separable. They peak just below h = 1 and decay as the chain polarizes. Around the peak the gap to E is widest. The reason is physical. Close to the critical point the correlation length exceeds the size of the blocks, many Schmidt levels of comparable weight contribute, and the PT spectrum inherits their spread.
